When you look at the so called "first wave" of feminism, you are looking at the post WW2 days of the War reconstruction era and the rise of mass consumerism. We all have a version of what the 1950's countries standards of living were in that time, in an effort to "recover" from the horrors of WW2 - returning soldiers were encouraged to hide their PTSD, and start families as soon as possible. Women that were working on a war footing tasting the fruits of paid labor (such as Rosie the pop riverter/welder) and became independent were encouraged to head home have kids, and have ambitions out side the home curtailed and be content with the new role of "Housewife." This was because returning service men provided a glut of labor - and additional labor was not needed at this time.

When we look at the early 1960's and the beginning of feminism - it was initially a small group of women that were unhappy and curtailed due to the limits placed on them. Women at that time in the US were effectively fired from work places if they married or had a kid out of wedlock. In many countries it was illegal to be gay, and in the US the black civil rights - were also questioning the status quo. Women were seen as this reserve labor - underpaid for the same work as men, fired at will not offered contracts. See "Made in Dagenham" the movie http://www.imdb.com/title/tt1371155/ for a good example of how UK labor laws were like that in this era.

Ok so - the advent of the pill in the mid 60's changed how women relate to men for ever. I suspect when or if - Vasalgel finally becomes commercially available to men at the end of this decade it will also change the dynamics - which to be honest for the better really.

From the mid 60s as women could control their fertility - this meant that it was possible to limit families so having a career was a possibility, as was studying and getting a degree or a trade. This also meant that more labor was available for the work place and a higher standard of living was available to women for the first time. This was a boon for manually intensive crappy jobs - so that work became available to many women for the first time since WW2, abeit part time and patchy it was still well paid enough to allow a certain amount of freedom.

By the 90s - feminism had turned in to a rally cry around things not yet done - in many countries being "Gay" was/is illegal - plus Gay marriage was off the table for most countries then. The female pay gap of women earning $0.70 to a man's $1 still stubbornly stuck and women doing the crappy jobs because retraining was restricted to fluffy arts degrees and useless frippery and only the daughters of the wealthy can access a quality education, and the domestic abuse rates of women in relationships still a problem. These are still real and relevant problems today.

Currently we have what I would suggest is a poor cousin feminism as "Identity politics" feminism - or 3rd wave feminism that is a pre-occupation with labeling the exterior world around them, according to feelings and ignoring the true substance and real problems with society as "too hard."
